After the TCI, variable operating costs, and fixed operating costs are determined, a discounted cash flow rate of return analysis is typically used to determine MFSP. The discounted cash flow analysis was calculated by iterating the selling cost of the product until the net present value of the project is zero with a 10% internal rate of return. The analysis requires that the discount rate, depreciation method, income tax rates, plant life, and construction startup duration be specified. The discounted cash flow assumes 40% equity financing with a loan interest at 8% for 10 years. Working capital is assumed to be 5% of the fixed capital investment. The Internal Revenue Service Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System was used because it offered the shortest recovery period and largest tax deductions, consistent with several NLR design reports. The steam production plants depreciate over a 20-year recovery period, and all other properties depreciate in a 7-year recovery period. The plant’s life is assumed to be 30 years. Detailed methods are described in previously published NLR design reports (Humbird et al. 2011; Dutta et al. 2011; Davis et al. 2014). TCI per annual gallon of gasoline equivalent (gge) of fuel is also listed in the tables of this section. This parameter illustrates the challenges in capital investment. For example, although MFSP for both MSW and woody biomass to hydrocarbon fuels (HC, including SAF) pathways are low, the TCI/annual gge of fuel produced are high. This indicates significant capital investment would be required for constructing the biorefinery facilities. This partially explains why there is limited investment being made today in these technologies even though they are cost-competitive with economy of scale. Technology challenges and risks for large-scale commercialization for individual pathways have not been explored extensively in this report; this could be positioned as a logical future study. 2.2.1 Oils, Fats, Yellow Grease, Brown Grease, and Animal Fats Although feedstocks for HEFA processes include natural oils derived from plants, animal fats, postconsumer wastes (e.g., yellow grease), and aquatic microorganisms such as algae and cyanobacteria, the generic process concept is very similar.
